title: Assessing Financial Literacy Among College Student-Athletes
text_snippet: Assessing Financial Literacy Among College Student-Athletes Abstract: This study investigates the financial literacy of college student-athletes, a group facing unique financial challenges and opportunities, particularly with the growth of name, image, and likeness deals. Using data from the 2020 National Postsecondary Student Aid Study, this research compares the financial literacy levels of student-athletes to their non-athlete peers and explores the predictors of financial literacy within the student-athlete population. The findings reveal that student-athletes generally exhibit lower financial literacy than non-student-athletes, even after controlling for demographic and institutional factors. Additionally, significant disparities in financial literacy are observed based on gender, race, and institutional characteristics. These results underscore the need for targeted financial education programs tailored to the specific needs of student-athletes, particularly those from underrepresented groups. The study concludes with recommendations for universities and athletic programs to better support student-athletes in achieving financial competency.

title: Modeling Student Persistence in Online Education: A Validation Study
text_snippet: Modeling Student Persistence in Online Education: A Validation Study Abstract: This study examined the factors related to student persistence in online education programs. Using a model of persistence, we conducted five confirmatory factor analytic models to evaluate scales that measured the factors of interest: locus of control, self-efficacy, task value, satisfaction, and persistence. We also conducted and compared two structural equation models to investigate the relationships among these factors, along with achievement. Results indicated that the critical factors related to students' persistence in online programs are locus of control, self-efficacy, and achievement. On the other hand, task value and satisfaction were not significant predictors of online program persistence. The similarities and dissimilarities between previous findings and the present study are discussed.

title: Cultural Challenges and Adaptation: College Education Experiences of Chinese First-Generation College Students
text_snippet: Cultural Challenges and Adaptation: College Education Experiences of Chinese First-Generation College Students Abstract: Chinese first-generation college students (FGCS) experience cultural challenges. We developed a framework for analyzing the content of interviews with 20 Chinese FGCS in three college stages. In the input stage, narrow family perceptions misled the FGCS college goals, manifested as unrealistic visions or negative attitudes. In the shallow college environment stage, lack of family guidance hindered FGCS college transition, as shown through curriculum learning unpreparedness, information barriers during research activities, and two extremes of participation in extracurricular activities. In the deep college environment stage, mismatched family culture impeded FGCS college adaptation, as shown by instrumentalist attitude towards curriculum learning, fear of the teachers' authority when conducting research activities, and poor integration in extracurricular activities under the influence of weak cultural capital. It is necessary for colleges to provide "cognitive adjustment—experience compensation—cultural support" for FGCS, and more specifically, can provide direct support (internal and external support) and interpersonal interactions support (role-model, guidance, and resou

title: "Education Was Always My Ticket to Something More": Disabled Transfer Students' Educational Journeys Across Contexts
text_snippet: "Education Was Always My Ticket to Something More": Disabled Transfer Students' Educational Journeys Across Contexts Abstract: Scholarship on disability in higher education has unveiled the complications that students face in coming to terms with their disabilities and traversing college based on the ableist settings they inhabit. Nonetheless, the paths, priorities, and unique challenges depicted in the literature are often limited to one institutional setting. In this narrative inquiry study involving interviews with 14 pre- and post-transfer college students, we chronicle their journeys from high school to community college and, for some, to a post-transfer institution. In particular, we unveil how, over these three points in time, students engage in changes of how they reconcile their disabled identities and waver between independent and interdependent behaviors. Our findings call for further inquiry regarding the role of familial capital in informing students' resource attainment, as well as push practitioners to form more intentional partnerships to support disabled students' smoother transitions across educational institutions.

title: Understanding the Varying Salience of First-Gen Status for First-Generation College Students
text_snippet: Understanding the Varying Salience of First-Gen Status for First-Generation College Students Abstract: Our constructivist qualitative case study of first-generation college students at Research University analyzed 13 focus groups with 54 students. Our analysis revealed five identities and experiences that specifically shaped the salience of first-gen status for our participants. For participants with a sibling or from low-income families, first-gen status had variable salience depending on the nuances of those experiences. Having an immigrant background or transferring from a community college heightened first-gen status salience by creating a second layer of transition impacted by students' social and cultural capital. Racially and ethnically minoritized participants explicitly noted that race and ethnicity were more salient in their college experiences than first-gen status. The relationship between these aspects of salience and identity also reflected the RU context as a predominantly white, four-year, moderately priced institution. We conclude with implications for how institutions can further support first-gen students on campus while calling for the continued exploration of first-gen status.

title: Understanding College Access of Immigrant-Origin, Emergent Bilingual Learners
text_snippet: Understanding College Access of Immigrant-Origin, Emergent Bilingual Learners Abstract: Emergent bilingual learners (EBLs) comprise 10% of U.S. students, yet evidence less academic success as a group compared to their non-EBL counterparts. While research has documented the struggles of EBLs in pursuing post-secondary educational pathways, this qualitative study examines factors that are associated with successfully pursuing enrollment in 4-year colleges and universities. Eighteen EBL students participated in interviews about their journey toward college. Data were grouped into three main areas: motivations for pursuing college, assets contributing to success, and barriers experienced. Core themes in the data included the primary motivator of fulfilling family dreams; positive and negative contributions of teachers, counselors, and peers; positive influences of secondary curricular and extracurricular engagement; and ongoing linguistic challenges. Findings have implications for professionals who work with EBLs both prior to and during college to better support these students in their transition to college.

title: The Development of Sense of Campus Belonging: A Four-Year Longitudinal Study of Low-Income College Students
text_snippet: The Development of Sense of Campus Belonging: A Four-Year Longitudinal Study of Low-Income College Students Abstract: The study draws on longitudinal data covering four years of college among a sample of students from low-income backgrounds, with histories of adverse childhood experiences, who enrolled at more than 150 four-year institutions. Analyses investigate factors that influence the emergence and development of students' sense of campus belonging, with findings highlighting the importance that having a mentor plays in early college levels of sense of belonging, and the positive developmental effects of campus involvement over four years of college. Results indicate that first-generation students enter college disadvantaged in terms of their sense of belonging, which grows more pronounced over four years. Campus involvement appeared to exert a less positive influence in cultivating sense of belonging among first-generation students than among their continuing-generation counterparts. Because of the low-income characteristic of our sample, the disadvantages found among first-generation students may be attributable to the specific qualities that accompany being a first-generation college student, rather than broader notions of family income or social class.

title: "It's Not About Blood, It's About Who Shows Up for Me": Black College-going Foster Youth Disrupting Family Privilege and Creating Chosen Family Networks
text_snippet: "It's Not About Blood, It's About Who Shows Up for Me": Black College-going Foster Youth Disrupting Family Privilege and Creating Chosen Family Networks Abstract: Utilizing narrative inquiry, this study collected individual interviews to understand how nine Black students who experienced the carceral nexus of foster care navigated college. Utilizing BlackCrit and Community Cultural Wealth as a theoretical framework, findings show how the foster care system was dehumanizing and stripped students of their family privilege. Findings also show how the students resisted the foster care system by (re)defining family in their own way by creating chosen family. Lastly, findings show the unique ways their chosen families provided the love, care, and capital needed to thrive in college, they leaned on their chosen family as support throughout their college experiences. Implications focus on the ways in which family privilege operates in higher education and how it disadvantages Black foster youth. Recommendations focus on creating more inclusive and equitable spaces for Black students with foster care histories.

title: When Push Comes to Shove: (Dis)junctures in Utility, Purpose, and Meaning in White College Students' Intra-Racial Conversations About Race
text_snippet: When Push Comes to Shove: (Dis)junctures in Utility, Purpose, and Meaning in White College Students' Intra-Racial Conversations About Race Abstract: Prior scholarship has documented the experiences of white students engaging in racial dialogues in curricular and co-curricular contexts, however less research considers their conversations about race within their white peer and family networks, specifically within the context of anti-racist practice. This constructivist grounded theory study examined what white students' experiences having intra-racial conversations about race mean within their anti-racist practice and what, if anything, these conversations do. Our analysis revealed participants' divergent understandings of anti-racist practice and the various meanings they ascribed to their intra-racial conversations within that practice. Most participants operated through a lens that evaded the role of socially constructed power and de-centered People of Color, which significantly influenced how they conceptualized their anti-racist practice, the nature and purpose of their conversations, and their experiences within these conversations. title: Experiences of International Doctoral Student Mothers at a US Research University
text_snippet: Experiences of International Doctoral Student Mothers at a US Research University Abstract: Female doctoral students often experience several challenges in the program while balancing their personal and family roles. This phenomenological study investigated the experiences of international student mothers (N = 6) while pursuing full-time doctoral degrees, providing insights into how they navigate a research university. The study has one central research question: What are the daily life experiences of full-time international doctoral student mothers caring for their child/ren, pursuing a career, and researching in education? The findings highlight the importance of social support in the success and well-being of female international doctoral students.

title: College Students from Immigrant Families: Meaning Making about Identity and Intersectional Complexity
text_snippet: College Students from Immigrant Families: Meaning Making about Identity and Intersectional Complexity Abstract: College students from immigrant families (CSIF) make up a growing portion of undergraduate enrollment in U.S. colleges and universities. While emerging studies have made important progress in understanding the experiences, educational pathways, and navigational strategies of these students, CSIF are often neglected in research on college student development, a pattern that has consequences for practitioners’ opportunities to support student success. Drawing from 45 in-depth interviews with CSIF enrolled at a large public research university, this study examined how participants made meaning of their social location as part of the first generation in their family to grow up in the United States. Our findings show how students made meaning of CSIF identities by framing them as sources of (1) opportunities for social connection, (2) community cultural wealth, (3) family responsibility, and (4) intersectional complexity. These findings are presented alongside their implications for scholars of student development and practitioners who seek to support college students from immigrant families.

title: Sexual Orientation-Based Microaggressions, Coping Responses, and Adjustment to College
text_snippet: Sexual Orientation-Based Microaggressions, Coping Responses, and Adjustment to College Abstract: The relations between sexual orientation-based microaggressions and emotional, academic, and social adjustment to college were examined in 241 sexual minority persons who completed an online survey. The mediating roles of five coping responses to discrimination (detachment, internalization, drug and alcohol use, resistance, and education/ activism) were examined in these links. Sexual orientation-based microaggressions were negatively correlated with both emotional and academic adjustment to college at the bivariate level, and were indirectly related to emotional adjustment through coping via detachment, internalization, and drug and alcohol use. They were indirectly related to academic adjustment through coping via internalization, drug and alcohol use, and education/activism. Finally, sexual orientation- based microaggressions were indirectly related to social adjustment via detachment coping. title: Jewish Fraternity and Sorority Members’ Coping and Sensemaking Responses to Antisemitism
text_snippet: Jewish Fraternity and Sorority Members’ Coping and Sensemaking Responses to Antisemitism Abstract: Findings are presented from a national qualitative research study with members of traditionally Jewish fraternity and sorority chapters. It explores responses of Jewish students to a campus climate that, since October 7, 2023, has shifted to tension, confusion, and heightened emotion. In focus groups, Jewish students described personally experiencing and witnessing various forms of antisemitism—from everyday slights and social isolation to death threats and physical assaults. Students shared five main types of narratives by which they made sense and coped with these incidents: (1) resistance to antisemitism, (2) socially isolating or distancing from peers and campus communities, (3) minimizing or downplaying incidents of antisemitism, (4) psychologically engaging in hypervigilance around safety and security, and (5) masking their Judaism in public and social media spaces. Implications for practice include training for campus professionals around supporting Jewish students during this period of heightened stress and emotional strain.

title: Living the Major: A Grounded Model of Major and Career Choices for Disabled College Students
text_snippet: Living the Major: A Grounded Model of Major and Career Choices for Disabled College Students Abstract: Contemporary rhetoric about major and career choice often focuses on passion, interest, and personal agency. However, that can oversimplify decision making processes deeply intertwined with disability identity, health, and ableist barriers. Using data from a grounded theory study with 59 disabled college students, this article presents a model of Major and Career Choice for Disabled College Students.

title: The Course Planning Process of Practitioner-Adjuncts in HESA Master’s Programs
text_snippet: The Course Planning Process of Practitioner-Adjuncts in HESA Master’s Programs Abstract: This study explores how practitioner-adjuncts, full-time student affairs practitioners who serve as adjunct instructors in higher education/student affairs (HESA) Master’s programs, engage in course planning and preparation. Based on interviews with 28 practitioner-adjuncts, findings describe a model of course planning in which individuals pursue adjunct teaching based on several motivations. Their planning process first involves reviewing existing syllabi. It then involves interrelated considerations for objectives, content, and students focused on practical utility and application. Programmatic, institutional, and professional contextual influences further shape their decision-making. This study has implications for HESA programs that use adjunct instructors and further research on curriculum development in HESA programs.

title: Empowering Voices: The Role of a Writing Center in the Academic Success of International Doctoral Students
text_snippet: Empowering Voices: The Role of a Writing Center in the Academic Success of International Doctoral Students Abstract: This qualitative instrumental case study examines the role of a university Writing Center in supporting the academic success and socialization of international doctoral students at a public university in the Midwest. Guided by Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development and Lave and Wenger’s communities of practice frameworks, the study explores how sustained interactions with writing tutors influence students’ academic writing development and broader academic experiences. Data were collected through 17 semi-structured interviews and 15 tutoring session observations conducted during the Spring 2020 semester. Findings indicate that international doctoral students initially face challenges related to English proficiency, academic discourse conventions, and confidence in articulating their needs. Over time, scaffolded feedback and consistent tutor relationships fostered improved writing skills, increased academic confidence, and deeper integration into academic communities of practice. title: The Cost of Resilience: Navigating Disability-Related Financial Tradeoffs Amid Systemic Neglect in College
text_snippet: The Cost of Resilience: Navigating Disability-Related Financial Tradeoffs Amid Systemic Neglect in College Abstract: Students with disabilities confront disproportionate financial barriers in higher education, yet research has rarely explored how these students actively navigate disability-related expenses in pursuit of their degrees. This mixed methods study investigated experiences of 334 disabled undergraduates at four-year U.S. institutions, integrating survey data and 20 nested interviews to examine the specific tradeoffs students make between finances and physical health, mental health, and personal safety. Findings reveal that coping strategies surrounding medication costs, mental health care access, and transportation are pervasive, often arising from unmet financial need and gaps in institutional support. Implications highlight the need for postsecondary institutions and policymakers to extend financial aid, health service coverage, and coordinated support beyond minimal compliance, directly addressing the structural roots of inequity. This work advances resilience theory in disability in higher education literature by foregrounding the systemic costs of “resilience” and calls for a shift from celebrating coping to dismantling the conditions that necessitate such tradeoffs.
